title: Investigation of the use and integration of rhythm- and music-based interventions in routine physiotherapy practice and the factors influencing this process
summary:
Rhythm- and music-based treatment methods use music, rhythm, or other auditory cues to support movement and the learning of movement sequences. Examples include walking to the beat of a metronome or performing movement exercises to music. These methods are used particularly in the rehabilitation of people with neurological conditions such as Parkinson’s disease, multiple sclerosis, or following a stroke. Scientific studies have shown that certain rhythm- and music-based methods can improve mobility and walking ability.

Although these methods may have positive effects, little is currently known about how frequently they are actually used in everyday physiotherapy practice. It is also unclear which factors facilitate or hinder their use. These may include, for example, physiotherapists’ knowledge and experience, their attitudes towards these methods, and the available time and organisational resources.

The aim of the study is to identify the factors that facilitate or hinder the use of rhythm- and music-based treatment methods by physiotherapists in Germany, Austria, and Switzerland. In addition, the study aims to investigate the extent to which these methods have already become part of everyday physiotherapy practice and whether the perceived influencing factors differ between physiotherapists who already use these methods and those who do not currently use them.

The study consists of three consecutive parts.

In the first part, a scientific questionnaire designed to assess factors that may influence the use of treatment methods will be translated into German. A group of experts will review whether the questions are technically accurate, understandable, and appropriate for the language used in Germany, Austria, and Switzerland.

In the second part, the comprehensibility of the translated questionnaire will be assessed through individual online interviews with twelve physiotherapists from the three countries. Participants will be asked to explain how they understand the questions and will have the opportunity to identify any ambiguities. Based on their feedback, the questionnaire will be revised if necessary.

In the third part, an anonymous online survey will be conducted among approximately 500 practising physiotherapists from Germany, Austria, and Switzerland. Participation is voluntary and will take approximately 10 to 15 minutes. The survey will collect information about participants’ professional activities and their personal assessments of factors that influence the use of rhythm- and music-based treatment methods. Physiotherapists who already use these methods will answer additional questions about how well they have been integrated into their everyday professional practice. All participants will also have the opportunity to share their own experiences and suggestions.

The findings are expected to contribute to a better understanding of the conditions that influence the use of rhythm- and music-based treatment methods in physiotherapy. In the long term, they may help inform the development of appropriate measures to support the use of these methods in physiotherapy care.
conditions: Use and integration of rhythm- and music-based interventions (RMBI) into routine physiotherapy practice, including associated barriers and facilitators, within the field of implementation science.

interventions.name: The study consists of three consecutive phases: (1) the translation and cross-cultural adaptation of the t-DIBQ with the involvement of an expert committee (based on the COSMIN guidelines)
(2) Cognitive interviews with twelve physiotherapists from Germany, Austria, and Switzerland

(3) Anonymous quantitative online survey of physiotherapists in Germany, Austria, and Switzerland. No therapeutic interventions will be administered, and participants will not be randomly assigned to groups.

criteria:
Inclusion criteria:
(1) Experts
•	Minimum age of 26 years. 
•	Sufficient proficiency in German to assess the German-language questionnaire from a professional and linguistic perspective and to actively participate in expert committee discussions conducted in German.
•	Demonstrable expertise in at least one of the following areas:
o	Physiotherapy or health sciences,
o	Implementation science,
o	Translation and validation of measurement instruments,
o	COSMIN-based methodological procedures,
o	Linguistics (English and German).
•	Several years of relevant professional or research experience (generally at least five years) and/or specific professional qualifications in the respective area of expertise.
Expertise may additionally be demonstrated through scientific publications, research activities, participation in relevant projects or guideline development, or recognized professional roles. Not all of these forms of evidence are required simultaneously.
(2) Physiotherapists in cognitive interviews
•	Currently practicing as a physiotherapist.
•	Professional practice located in Germany, Austria, or Switzerland.
•	Sufficient proficiency in German to independently understand and respond to the German-language questionnaire and the questions asked during the cognitive interview.
(3) Physiotherapists in Online Survey
•	Currently practicing as a physiotherapist.
•	Professional practice located in Germany, Austria, or Switzerland.
•	Sufficient proficiency in German to independently understand and complete the German-language online questionnaire.
Previous use of rhythm- and music-based interventions (RMBI) is not required for participation in the cognitive interviews or the online survey. Both RMBI users and non-users are eligible to participate.
Exclusion criteria:
(1) Experts
•	Insufficient proficiency in German to assess the German-language questionnaire from a professional and linguistic perspective or to actively participate in Expert Committee discussions conducted in German.
•	Failure to meet the professional inclusion criteria defined for the respective area of expertise.
Living or working in a non-German-speaking region of Switzerland does not, in itself, constitute an exclusion criterion.
(2) Physiotherapists in cognitive interviews
•	Not currently practicing as a physiotherapist.
•	Professional practice located outside Germany, Austria, or Switzerland.
•	Insufficient proficiency in German to independently understand and respond to the German-language questionnaire and the questions asked during the cognitive interview.
Living or working in a French-, Italian-, or Romansh-speaking region of Switzerland does not, in itself, constitute an exclusion criterion, provided that sufficient proficiency in German is demonstrated.
(3) Physiotherapists in online survey
•	Not currently practicing as a physiotherapist.
•	Professional practice located outside Germany, Austria, or Switzerland.
•	Insufficient proficiency in German to independently understand and complete the German-language questionnaire.
Living or working in a French-, Italian-, or Romansh-speaking region of Switzerland does not, in itself, constitute an exclusion criterion, provided that sufficient proficiency in German is demonstrated.
